rules.name: Epsilon definition of sequence limit
rules.output_form: for every epsilon > 0 there exists N with |a_n-L| < epsilon for n >= N
preconditions: The sequence and candidate limit are real-valued
rules.operation: Express sequence convergence through the epsilon-N definition.
examples: The sequence 1/n converges to 0 by making n large enough to force 1/n below any epsilon
counterexamples: Checking the inequality for only finitely many indices is invalid

rules.name: Monotone bounded convergence rule
preconditions: The sequence is monotone and bounded in R
rules.operation: Conclude convergence of a monotone bounded sequence in the real numbers.
examples: An increasing sequence bounded above has a real limit
counterexamples: Monotonicity alone without boundedness does not ensure convergence in R

rules.name: Cauchy criterion seed
preconditions: The sequence is interpreted in the complete real metric
rules.operation: Use completeness of the real numbers to identify convergence with the Cauchy property.
examples: Completeness of R converts Cauchy control into actual convergence
counterexamples: Using the criterion in an incomplete space without extra hypotheses is invalid

rules.name: Epsilon-delta continuity definition
rules.output_form: for every epsilon > 0 there exists delta > 0 with |f(x)-f(x_0)| < epsilon when |x-x_0| < delta
preconditions: The function is defined near x_0
rules.operation: Express pointwise continuity using the epsilon-delta criterion.
examples: Polynomial functions satisfy the epsilon-delta continuity condition at every real point
counterexamples: Checking continuity only on one side when two-sided continuity is required is invalid

rules.name: Intermediate value theorem seed
rules.output_form: attains every intermediate value between endpoint values
preconditions: The function is continuous on the relevant interval
rules.operation: Use continuity on an interval to guarantee intermediate values.
examples: If f(a) < 0 < f(b), then some c between a and b satisfies f(c) = 0
counterexamples: Applying the theorem to a discontinuous function is invalid

rules.name: Heine-Borel compactness rule
preconditions: The subset is interpreted in the standard real topology
rules.operation: Classify compact subsets of the real line by closedness and boundedness.
examples: A closed interval [a,b] is compact in the real line
counterexamples: An open interval is bounded but not compact in R

rules.name: Bolzano-Weierstrass rule
preconditions: The sequence is bounded in R
rules.operation: Extract a convergent subsequence from a bounded real sequence.
examples: Bounded oscillating sequences still admit convergent subsequences
counterexamples: Unbounded sequences do not satisfy the theorem hypotheses

rules.name: Uniform continuity on compact intervals
rules.input_form: continuous function on a compact interval
preconditions: The function is continuous on a compact interval
rules.operation: Promote pointwise continuity to uniform continuity on compact intervals.
examples: Continuous functions on [0,1] admit one delta choice that works across the whole interval
counterexamples: Continuity on a noncompact domain does not imply uniform continuity in general

rules.name: Limsup and liminf order rule
preconditions: Limsup and liminf are interpreted in the extended real sense
rules.operation: Order the lower and upper asymptotic limits of a sequence.
examples: Oscillating bounded sequences may have distinct liminf and limsup values framing their subsequential limits
counterexamples: Reversing the inequality is invalid

rules.name: Ratio test seed
rules.input_form: series sum a_n with ratio limit L
rules.output_form: absolute convergence if L < 1 and divergence if L > 1
preconditions: The relevant ratio limit exists in the stated form
rules.operation: Classify many series by the limiting size ratio of successive terms.
examples: Geometric-type tails are classified effectively by the ratio test
counterexamples: The ratio test is inconclusive in general when L = 1

rules.name: Arzela-Ascoli seed
rules.input_form: equibounded equicontinuous family on a compact domain
rules.output_form: uniformly convergent subsequence exists under the standard hypotheses
preconditions: The family is defined on a compact domain and satisfies the standard equicontinuity and boundedness hypotheses
rules.operation: Extract a uniformly convergent subsequence from a controlled family of functions.
examples: Compactness of function families can be proved by controlling both oscillation and size on compact sets
counterexamples: Pointwise boundedness without equicontinuity is insufficient in general

rules.name: Absolute convergence implies convergence
preconditions: sum |a_n| converges
rules.operation: Promote absolute summability to ordinary convergence.
examples: Alternating or signed terms become harmless once the absolute series is summable
counterexamples: Conditional convergence does not imply absolute convergence

rules.name: Power series radius rule
rules.output_form: radius of convergence R with absolute convergence inside and divergence outside
preconditions: The series is interpreted in the standard one-variable power-series setting
rules.operation: Classify power-series convergence by a radius parameter.
examples: Coefficient growth determines a sharp analytic disk or interval of convergence through the radius parameter
counterexamples: Behavior at boundary points cannot be inferred from the radius alone in general

rules.name: Differentiability implies continuity rule
preconditions: The derivative exists at the point under consideration
rules.operation: Use derivative existence to force continuity.
examples: Derivative existence gives a first-order approximation strong enough to force local continuity
counterexamples: Continuity alone does not imply differentiability

rules.name: Fundamental theorem of calculus seed
rules.input_form: integral and antiderivative data under the standard regularity hypotheses
rules.output_form: differentiation and integration invert one another in the basic one-variable setting
preconditions: The active continuity and integrability hypotheses hold
rules.operation: Relate antiderivatives, accumulated-area functions, and definite integrals.
examples: Antiderivative structure converts integrals into endpoint evaluation and accumulated-area functions into derivatives
